notes.meaning: Jonathan, Saul's son, quietly plans a daring attack on the enemy outpost with only his armor-bearer. He does not tell his father, likely because Saul would have stopped him. Breaking army rules like this would normally be wrong, but older commentators think God was stirring Jonathan to act. Through this, God would show Israel that victory comes from his grace, not from big numbers or weapons.

Meanwhile King Saul sits under a pomegranate tree at the edge of Gibeah. He has only about six hundred men left, not the three thousand he once had. Saul seems stuck and unsure what to do, because he has lost God's favor. People who know they have turned from God's protection never feel safe.

With Saul is Ahijah, a great-grandson of the old priest Eli. He wears the ephod, the high priest's special vest used when asking God for guidance. He is probably the same man later called Ahimelech. Saul, who had been scolded by Samuel, now keeps a priest close, hoping outward religion will make things right with God. No one in camp knows Jonathan has slipped away.

The path to the enemy runs through a deep valley between two steep, tooth-like cliffs. One was called Bozez, which may mean "shining" or "slippery." The other was Seneh, "thorny." One faced the Philistines at Michmash and the other faced Israel's side. The hard climb did not scare Jonathan off. It only made him more determined.

Jonathan calls the Philistines "uncircumcised." He means they are outside God's covenant, God's binding promise to his people. His "perhaps" is not doubt in God's power. It is humility: success is in God's hands, not his own. He holds on to a great truth: nothing stops the Lord from saving, whether he uses many people or only a few.

The armor-bearer gives a loyal answer: "I'm with you all the way." He will follow Jonathan wherever he goes and share every danger. Matthew Henry says he seemed to carry not just Jonathan's weapons but his heart. His support gave Jonathan fresh courage.

Jonathan asks God for a sign, much like Abraham's servant did when he was looking for a wife for Isaac. If the enemy says "Wait there," the two will stay put. If they say "Come up," that will show the enemy is afraid to come down and fight, and that God has given them into Israel's hand. The older commentators believe God's Spirit put this sign in Jonathan's heart. It shows that God can guide even the words of people who do not know him.

The two men step into plain view. The Philistines mock them: "Look, the Hebrews are crawling out of their holes!" They likely took the pair for deserters, not attackers, so they did nothing to stop them climbing up.

The guards shout a scornful dare: "Come on up, and we'll teach you a lesson!" This was exactly the sign Jonathan had asked for. His "perhaps" now turns into confidence. He says God has handed them over "to Israel," not "to us," because he wanted the good of his people, not glory for himself.

Jonathan scrambles up the rock on hands and feet, with his armor-bearer right behind. Jonathan struck the enemy down, and his armor-bearer finished them off. The Philistines were stunned by such boldness. God also filled them with panic.

In this first strike, the two men killed about twenty soldiers in a very small space. That space is about half of what a pair of oxen could plow in a day. The enemy above could not see how many Israelites might be coming, so they fled in fear. The victory began with Jonathan's faith, but the outcome came from God.

Terror spreads through the whole Philistine army, even its toughest raiders. The words behind "panic from God" mean the fear was more than normal fright. God himself sent it, and the ground shook as well. As Matthew Henry puts it, the One who made the heart knows how to make it tremble.
From Gibeah, Saul's lookouts see the huge enemy army "melting away." Soldiers are scattering in every direction and striking one another. They melted like snow before the sun, by God's power.

Saul guesses someone from his own small army must be causing the uproar, so he calls a roll. Only Jonathan and his armor-bearer are missing. That made it plain the victory was the Lord's doing. Two men alone could never have done so much.

Saul tells the priest to bring the ark of God, the sacred chest that stood for God's presence. He wants to ask God whether he should attack. Matthew Henry warns that many people ask God about their safety who never ask him about their duty.

While the priest is still asking God, the noise in the enemy camp grows louder. So Saul tells him, "Withdraw your hand," which means "Stop. There's no time." Saul thought the answer was obvious, and he was too hasty to wait for God. A person of faith never treats any business as so urgent that there is no time to take God along.

Saul gathers his men with shouts and rushes to the battle. He finds the Philistines in total confusion, killing one another with their own swords. The weapons they trusted became the tools of their downfall, as happened in Gideon's day.

Some Hebrews had been living or serving among the Philistines. Some may have been servants. Others had sided with the enemy out of fear or to win their favor. Now they switch back to Israel's side. That added even more confusion in the Philistine camp.

Israelites who had fled and hidden in the hills hear the enemy is running, and they come out to join the chase. Coming only once the danger had passed was not much to their credit. Still, it would have been worse if they had not come at all.
The writer makes the main point clear: the LORD saved Israel that day. The people did the fighting, but God did the saving through them. Without him they could do nothing. Rescue comes from the Lord.

Saul puts a curse on any soldier who eats before evening, so the enemy cannot escape. He may have meant well, but the order was harsh and unwise. It saved time but drained his men's strength, so it worked against his own goal. Notice he says "my enemies." Saul was thinking more of himself than of God's cause.
As the tired army chases the enemy, they come into a forest. There, wild honey is dripping onto the ground. Bees in that land often lived wild in trees and rocks. The land truly flowed with honey.

Even with sweet food right in front of them, not one hungry soldier takes a taste. They are afraid of the curse and its punishment. Matthew Henry praises people who can say no to their own cravings for fear of doing wrong. Still, Saul's rash order kept his men hungry for no good reason.
